interactions.label: Peripheral oedema caused by amlodipine is due to fluid retention and should be t

params.question: Peripheral oedema caused by amlodipine is due to fluid retention and should be treated with diuretics.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Amlodipine-induced oedema is caused by arteriolar vasodilation, not fluid overload. Diuretics are ineffective here; the correct approach is dose reduction or switching to another antihypertensive class.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct! Amlodipine-induced pedal oedema results from precapillary arteriolar vasodilation raising capillary hydrostatic pressure — not fluid retention. It is dose-dependent, affecting up to 40% of patients at high doses, and does not respond to diuretics. Dose reduction or switching to another class is the appropriate step.

interactions.label: A 52-year-old man on enalapril for diabetic nephropathy develops a persistent dr

params.question: A 52-year-old man on enalapril for diabetic nephropathy develops a persistent dry cough. His physician switches him to losartan. Which pharmacological property of ARBs best explains why they do not cause this cough?

answers.text: ARBs have a shorter half-life, reducing prolonged airway irritation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Half-life does not explain the cough. ACE inhibitor–induced cough is caused by bradykinin accumulation due to inhibition of its degradation, not by duration of drug exposure.

answers.text: ARBs block the AT2 receptor, which mediates the cough reflex

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: ARBs selectively block the AT1 receptor, not AT2. Angiotensin II still stimulates the unblocked AT2 receptor, which actually promotes beneficial vasodilation.

answers.text: ARBs do not inhibit bradykinin breakdown, so bradykinin does not accumulate in the airways

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! ACE inhibitors block both the conversion of angiotensin I to II and the degradation of bradykinin. Accumulated bradykinin irritates airway sensory nerve endings, causing cough. ARBs bypass this pathway entirely by acting downstream at the AT1 receptor.

answers.text: ARBs are prodrugs activated in the liver, avoiding pulmonary first-pass effects

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not all ARBs are prodrugs, and hepatic activation does not explain the absence of cough. The key difference is that ARBs do not affect bradykinin metabolism at all.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the dual action of ACE: it converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II AND degrades bradykinin. ACE inhibitors block both pathways, causing bradykinin to accumulate and trigger cough. ARBs act downstream at the AT1 receptor and leave bradykinin metabolism untouched.
Well done! The absence of bradykinin accumulation is the key pharmacological distinction that makes ARBs better tolerated than ACE inhibitors with respect to cough.

interactions.label: A patient with recurrent calcium oxalate renal stones and co-existing hypertensi

params.question: A patient with recurrent calcium oxalate renal stones and co-existing hypertension requires a diuretic. Which class is most appropriate?

answers.text: Loop diuretics, because they are the most potent and effectively reduce fluid load

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Loop diuretics block the NKCC2 transporter in the thick ascending limb and increase urinary calcium excretion (cause hypocalcaemia). This would worsen calcium stone disease by raising the filtered calcium load in the urine.

answers.text: Thiazide diuretics, because they reduce urinary calcium excretion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Thiazides act on the early distal convoluted tubule and enhance calcium reabsorption, lowering urinary calcium. This makes them uniquely suited for preventing calcium stones while simultaneously treating hypertension.

answers.text: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, because they alkalinise the urine and dissolve stones

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Acetazolamide alkalinises urine, which helps prevent uric acid stones, not calcium oxalate stones. It also produces only weak diuresis and causes metabolic acidosis.

answers.text: Potassium-sparing diuretics, because they prevent the hypokalaemia that promotes stone formation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While hypokalaemia can indirectly increase calcium excretion, potassium-sparing diuretics do not directly reduce urinary calcium. Thiazides are the evidence-based choice for calcium stone prevention.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the key calcium distinction: loop diuretics waste calcium (cause hypocalcaemia), while thiazides retain calcium (can cause hypercalcaemia). For calcium stone prevention, you need reduced urinary calcium — that means thiazides.
Excellent! Thiazides are the only diuretic class that reduces urinary calcium — a direct consequence of their site of action at the early DCT, where they enhance calcium reabsorption.

interactions.label: A patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is on maximum tolera

params.question: A patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is on maximum tolerated carvedilol, but the resting heart rate remains 82 bpm. Which drug should be added to reduce heart rate without weakening cardiac contraction?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Digoxin does slow heart rate through vagal enhancement and AV nodal effects, but it also has a narrow therapeutic index and does not selectively target heart rate. In this specific scenario — HR above 70 bpm on maximum beta-blocker — ivabradine is the targeted first-line add-on.

Diltiazem is a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker with significant negative inotropic effects. It is contraindicated in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction because it worsens pump failure.

Correct! Ivabradine selectively blocks the If (funny) current in SA node pacemaker cells, reducing heart rate without any negative inotropic effect. It is specifically indicated when the heart rate exceeds 70 bpm despite maximum tolerated beta-blocker therapy in HFrEF.
Verapamil has strong negative inotropic and chronotropic effects. Like diltiazem, it is contraindicated in HFrEF because it further depresses an already weakened myocardium.

overallFeedback.feedback: In HFrEF, many rate-slowing drugs are contraindicated because they also weaken contraction (negative inotropy). Ivabradine is unique: it acts only on the SA node's funny current, reducing rate without affecting the force of contraction.

Well done! Ivabradine's unique mechanism — pure heart rate reduction without affecting contractility — makes it the ideal add-on when beta-blockers alone cannot bring heart rate below 70 bpm in HFrEF.

interactions.label: In Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome with atrial fibrillation, verapamil can precip

params.question: In Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome with atrial fibrillation, verapamil can precipitate ventricular fibrillation. Which mechanism best explains this danger?

answers.text: Verapamil directly accelerates conduction velocity through the accessory pathway

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Verapamil does not directly affect the accessory pathway. The danger lies in what happens indirectly — blocking the AV node removes the safer conduction route and leaves the accessory pathway as the sole rapidly conducting conduit.

answers.text: Verapamil blocks AV nodal conduction, diverting all fibrillatory impulses through the unblocked accessory pathway at rates up to 250–350 bpm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! By blocking the AV node, verapamil eliminates the normal rate-limiting conduction pathway. Atrial fibrillatory impulses then travel exclusively through the accessory pathway, which lacks the AV node's protective delay, driving ventricular rates of 250–350 bpm that can degenerate into VF.

answers.text: Verapamil prolongs the QT interval, predisposing to torsades de pointes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: QT prolongation is associated with Class IA and Class III antiarrhythmics (e.g., quinidine, amiodarone), not with verapamil. The danger in WPW with AF is about conduction pathway diversion, not repolarisation delay.

answers.text: Verapamil causes profound vasodilation and hypotension, reducing coronary perfusion below a critical threshold

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While verapamil does cause some vasodilation, the life-threatening danger in WPW with AF is specifically the uncontrolled ventricular rate via the accessory pathway, not haemodynamic collapse from vasodilation.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical concept: four drugs (verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, adenosine) block the AV node but leave the accessory pathway wide open. With the AV node blocked, fibrillatory impulses race through the accessory pathway at 250–350 bpm, which can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. Safe alternatives are amiodarone, procainamide, or DC cardioversion.

Excellent analysis! The safe alternatives — amiodarone (prolongs refractoriness in the accessory pathway), procainamide, or DC cardioversion — work precisely because they block conduction through the accessory pathway rather than just the AV node.
